newsitem.title: UK: Hesitancy besets gold market at start of week.
newsitem.headline: Hesitancy besets gold market at start of week.

text.p: Gold starts Monday stuck for direction after hitting three-year lows last week and then, on Friday, gyrating wildly in the wake of comments from U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.
Greenspan's comments that the Fed must be wary of "irrational exuberance" in asset markets prompted short covering that picked gold off its lows.
"Anything that upsets calm in the financial markets is good for gold but gold was going up anyway before Greenspan spoke," said bullion analyst Andy Smith at Union Bank of Switzerland.

Financial markets in the far East and Europe fell as they took the remarks as meaning that the Fed might take action, and gold was propelled upwards as the professionals anticipated "hot" money seeking a safe haven in gold.
But benign U.S. inflation data last Friday ensured the Dow's fall was limited and gold prices quickly retreated.
"It was all about Wall Street on Friday afternoon," said one gold dealer.
As the excitement seemed to subside, gold's overall tone remained bearish with the spectre of sales from central bank reserves continuing to cow the market.
Steady selling by producers anxious to protect their income in a falling market and persistent rumours that European central banks had sold were likely to keep the price under pressure, dealers said.
On Wednesday the central banks of Portugal and Belgium formally denied they had sold gold from reserves.

But UBS's Smith predicted a volatile time ahead. "Gold shares have been bubbling and currencies are so volatile that one day producers are buying and the next selling. On top of that we have had short covering in an oversold market," he said.
The market could "just possibly absorb a lot more official sales," according to market reserachers CRU International.

"For all the talk of central bank activity sales from official sources have not been that large and they have barely offset the decline in gold exported by the Russian authorities," December's CRU Precious Metals Monitor said.

Gold coming on to the market from Russia, the central banks and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) during the 1990s had little more than averaged that during the 1980s and was less than the figures seen in the 1970s.
"Whether it can absorb more talk of them (official sales) is another matter," the report said.
It also noted that most recent producer sales were coming from Australia after the cherished level of A$500 per ounce had not been achieved.
With consumer interest still subdued, CRU forecast prices in a range "no better" than $355-$375 in the near term.
"In today's nervous market, psychology can turn quickly. The mere absence of bad news would allow prices to stabilise, consumer confidence to rebuild and buyers to return," the report said.
